# kis (keep-in-secret)

> kis lets a team commit secret files (`.env` and any other path listed in
> `.gitencrypt`) to git **encrypted**. It is a git clean/smudge filter: `git add`
> encrypts, checkout decrypts, so the working copy is plaintext while the index,
> history and remote only hold ciphertext. Works with any language or stack.

Install (needs git 2.28+): `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/juanfraherrero/keep-in-secret/main/install.sh | sh` (macOS/Linux), or `go install github.com/juanfraherrero/keep-in-secret/cmd/kis@latest`

## Rules for coding agents in a kis repository

A repository uses kis if it has a `.kis/` directory and a `.gitencrypt` file.

- Committing `.env` (and every file matched by `.gitencrypt`) is safe and expected.
  Do NOT add these files to `.gitignore`, `git rm` them, or move their values
  elsewhere to protect them. kis already does.
- Before every push or pull request, run `kis status --check`. Exit 0 means safe
  to push; exit 1 means a secret would leave in plaintext, and the output prints
  the fix. For a pull request use `kis status --check --since origin/main`.
- "Safe to push" covers only files matched by `.gitencrypt`; kis does not scan
  other files for hardcoded secrets.
- Use `kis status --json` to read state as data. Fields: `initialized`,
  `safe_to_push`, `encrypted_files`, `unlocked`, `files[].state` (`encrypted`, `plaintext-index`,
  `plaintext-head`, `wrong-group`, `untracked`, `ignored`; plus `group`,
  `readable`), `groups[]` and `problems[]` with `severity`
  (`error` blocks a push, `warning` does not), `path`, `commit`, `message`, `fix`.
- To encrypt another file: add its path to `.gitencrypt` (gitignore syntax), then
  run `kis sync`. Never edit the kis block of `.gitattributes` by hand.
- A secret file that is binary and starts with the bytes `\0KIS\0v1\0` means
  this clone is locked. `kis unlock` needs the developer's private key; ask
  them rather than working around it.
- If the developer's private key is not in a standard place (`$KIS_IDENTITY`,
  `~/.config/kis/identity`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, `~/.ssh/id_rsa`), run
  `kis unlock --identity PATH`, where PATH is their **private** key file (ask
  them for the path; never guess or search for keys). kis does not remember
  it: pass it on every `kis unlock`, or have the developer set
  `KIS_IDENTITY=PATH`, which creating a group (`@GROUP`) also needs.
  `kis init --identity PATH` takes the same private key file, not a `.pub`.
- On CI or a cloud agent, `kis unlock` reads the private key from the
  `KIS_PRIVATE_KEY` environment variable. If it is missing, ask the developer
  to run `kis add NAME --new-key` and store the printed key as that secret;
  never move secret values into the platform's own variables to bypass kis.
- A line ending in `@GROUP` (e.g. `.env.production @prod`) encrypts those files
  for that group only. Files of a group this clone isn't in stay ciphertext:
  that is expected, commit around them; never try to decrypt or recreate them.
  Access: `kis add NAME --group GROUP` (run by a member of that group).
- Don't copy secret values into code, logs, commit messages, PRs or chat.

## Setting kis up (non-interactive)

Every prompt takes its default without a terminal; `-y` forces it.

```sh
kis init -y --name NAME              # creates .gitencrypt, key, AGENTS.md section
                                     # NAME: how partners will see the developer (committed);
                                     # without --name, the git email before the @ is used
kis init -y --name NAME --preset terraform,android
git commit -m "Set up kis encryption" && git push
kis add PARTNER age1…|github:USER|key.pub   # then commit and push
kis unlock                           # partner, after cloning
kis add ci --new-key [--group G]     # CI / cloud agent: store the printed key as KIS_PRIVATE_KEY
KIS_PRIVATE_KEY=… kis unlock         # on that machine
```

## Stacks that don't use .env

`kis init` detects these and prints `kis sync --preset NAME`; it never applies
them unasked, because encrypting files CI reads in plaintext must be deliberate.

- `android`: `*.jks`, `*.keystore`, `keystore.properties`
- `rails`: `config/master.key`, `config/credentials/*.key`
- `spring`: `application-local.properties`, `application-local.yml`, `application-local.yaml`
- `terraform`: `*.tfvars`, `*.tfvars.json` (not `*.tfvars.example`)

Go, Rust, Python, Node, PHP and Ruby usually load `.env`, which the default
`.gitencrypt` covers. Any other file is one line in `.gitencrypt`.

## Commands

- `kis init [--identity PATH] [--name NAME] [--preset LIST] [--no-agents] [-y]`: set up encryption
- `kis status [--check] [--json] [--since REV]`: state and whether it is safe to push
- `kis sync [--preset LIST]`: apply `.gitencrypt` edits and re-encrypt
- `kis add NAME [KEY|github:USER|FILE.pub|--new-key] [--group G]`: give a partner access, optionally to a group; `--new-key` makes a key for CI or a cloud agent. `github:USER` grants access to every ed25519/RSA key on that GitHub account, read once; for a single key, ask the person for it
- `kis remove NAME [--group G] [--no-rotate]`: revoke and rotate the affected keys
- `kis rotate [--group G]`: new key(s), re-encrypt
- `kis unlock [--identity PATH]` (or `KIS_PRIVATE_KEY`) / `kis lock [--force]`: decrypt / re-encrypt this clone
- `kis keygen`, `kis pubkey`: personal key management. Accepted keys: age (`age1…`), SSH ed25519, SSH RSA; ECDSA and security keys (`sk-`) are refused
